name: Roast chicken
note: Rub under the skin, not only on it, and salt at least an hour ahead.

name: Lamb skewers
note: Season over the fire in two passes rather than once before, so the cumin toasts on the meat.

name: Pork ribs
note: Sugar-heavy rubs need an oven under 160C or a cool side of the grill.

name: Braised beef
note: Whole spices in a bag for a clear broth; ground spices if you want a thick sauce.

name: Steak
note: Coarse pepper burns on a hot pan. Press it on after searing, or use a moderate heat.

name: Venison or game
note: Resinous spices cut through gamey fat better than warm sweet ones.

name: Pâté or terrine
note: You cannot taste a raw mix, so weigh the spice against the meat rather than guessing.

name: Jerk chicken
note: Marinate overnight with lime and oil. The dry rub alone is only half the dish.

name: Grilled pork belly
note: Fat carries spice, so you need less than you would on a lean cut.

name: Roast duck
note: Season the cavity as well as the skin; the fat renders and carries it through.

name: Chicken tikka
note: The yoghurt is not optional. It carries the spice and tenderises at the same time.

name: Butter chicken
note: Tandoori for the marinade, garam masala stirred in at the end. Two blends, two stages.

name: Shawarma wrap
note: Oil and lemon in the marinade, then high heat and a little char.

name: Kofta
note: Mix the spice into the raw meat and rest it an hour so it distributes.

name: Doro wat
note: Bloom the berbere in a lot of onion and butter first. Undercook that step and the dish stays raw and harsh.

name: Kitfo
note: Served at the table with the spice alongside, not mixed in ahead.

name: Cochinita pibil
note: Loosen the rub with sour orange or lime into a paste before it touches the pork.

name: Chicken mole
note: The spice base is a third of the sauce. It still needs stock, tomato, fat and time.

name: Chili con carne
note: Bloom the powder in the rendered fat before the tomatoes go in.

name: Tacos
note: Add a splash of water with the spice so it becomes a glaze rather than dust.

name: Meatballs
note: Season the mix, then fry one small piece to taste before rolling the rest.

name: Pan-fried fish
note: Season the flesh side only; the skin side needs a dry surface to crisp.

name: Prawns
note: They cook in three minutes, so the spice has to be on before, not after.

name: Crab or shrimp boil
note: Salt the water hard and add the blend to the pot, not to the shell.

name: Prawn cocktail
note: Horseradish heat dies in a hot pan, so this only works cold.

name: Whole grilled fish
note: Score the flesh to the bone so the spice reaches past the skin.

name: Dal
note: Two spice moments: whole seeds popped in fat at the start, ground blend stirred in at the end.

name: Sambar
note: The tamarind goes in after the lentils are soft, or they never break down.

name: Rasam
note: Never boil it hard once the blend is in; a bare simmer keeps the pepper aromatic.

name: Chickpea stew
note: Chickpeas take a lot of spice. Start at the recommended dose and expect to add more.

name: Black beans
note: Bloom the blend in oil first; dumping it into the pot water leaves it flat.

name: Georgian bean stew
note: Add the blend late. The dried herbs in it lose everything to a long boil.

name: Hummus
note: Spice goes on top with the oil, not blended in, so each spoonful gets both.

name: Roast potatoes
note: Ground spice burns over a 40 minute roast. Add it in the last ten minutes.

name: Roast cauliflower
note: Toss with enough oil to carry the spice, or it sits on the surface and scorches.

name: Roast squash
note: The clearest demonstration that sweet spices work in savoury food.

name: Roast aubergine
note: Aubergine absorbs oil and spice together. Season the oil first, then brush.

name: Mushrooms
note: Wait until the water has cooked off before the spice goes in, or it steams instead of toasting.

name: Grilled corn
note: Butter or mayonnaise first so the powder has something to hold on to.

name: Vegetable curry
note: Curry powder at the start in fat, garam masala at the end off the heat.

name: Vegetable tagine
note: A long slow braise, so the blend can go in early and still hold.

name: Tofu
note: Tofu has no fat of its own, so the spice needs oil to travel.

name: Kimchi fried rice
note: The kimchi is already salty and sour. Cut the blend's salt accordingly.

name: Fried rice
note: Five-spice is easy to overdo in a fast dish. Half the usual dose is a safe start.

name: Couscous
note: Stir the blend into warm oil or butter before the grain goes in.

name: Persian rice
note: Steep the saffron separately in warm water and pour it over the finished rice.

name: Udon or soba
note: A table condiment. Put the jar out and let people dose it themselves.

name: Hot pot
note: Dry dip only works if it stays dry. Give each person their own small dish.

name: Pho broth
note: Char the spices and the aromatics dry before the bones go in. That colour is the flavour.

name: Chicken soup
note: One of the few blends that gains from a long simmer rather than fading.

name: Pumpkin soup
note: Bloom the blend in the butter you sweat the onion in.

name: Tomato sauce
note: A pinch of cassia in tomato sauce is the classic proof that warm spices belong in savoury food.

name: Pizza
note: On the sauce before baking, never on the cheese, where dried herbs burn.

name: Flatbread with oil
note: Oil first, blend second. Dry blend on dry bread just falls off.

name: Labneh or yoghurt dip
note: Scatter on top at the last moment so the texture survives.

name: Omelette
note: Fines herbes go in off the heat. Cooked, they turn to hay.

name: Scrambled eggs
note: Eggs are bland and fatty, which makes them the best place to taste a blend honestly.

name: Quick pickles
note: Whole spices only, so you can strain them out later.

name: Masala chai
note: Simmer in the milk rather than steeping in water. Fat extracts more than water does.

name: Mulled wine
note: Keep it below a simmer. Boiling pulls tannin out of the bark and turns it bitter.

name: Porridge or oats
note: Add it to the milk as it heats, not to the bowl at the end.

name: Gingerbread
note: Baked goods lose volatile aroma in the oven, so dose about a third higher than for a pan dish.

name: Fruit chaat
note: Sour and salty on sweet fruit. Add it at the table or the fruit weeps.

name: Thai grilled chicken
note: Make it a paste with oil and fish sauce, then marinate for at least four hours.
